reply: Funerals are for the living, and missing one leaves a gap where the goodbye should have been. It does not mean you did not love her, and it was not really your decision. You can still hold a goodbye of your own: visit later, light a lamp, write her the letter you would have said out loud. Late is allowed.[CHIPS]How do I start|I feel guilty|Tell my family[/CHIPS]

prompt: my riding instructor died and i havent been able to go back to the stable since
reply: The stable is full of him, so avoiding it makes complete sense right now. Do not force a return, but do not let it become permanent by accident either. Going back once with someone beside you, a parent or another rider, usually turns the place from unbearable to bittersweet. There is no deadline for that visit.[CHIPS]I feel nervous|Is that normal|What if I cry[/CHIPS]

prompt: is it normal that i feel more upset about my cat than about my great uncle
reply: Yes, and it is more common than people admit. Grief follows closeness and daily contact, not family trees. Your cat was in your room every night; your great uncle may have been a few visits a year. Feeling less about him is not disrespect, and there is no scoreboard you are failing.[CHIPS]Is that common|I feel guilty|What helps[/CHIPS]

prompt: nobody warns you that ordinary tuesday afternoons become the hard part
reply: That is one of the truest things about it. The big days get braced for and supported; the unremarkable ones catch you with no defences up. It helps to have something small already placed in the week: a walk, a friend you message on a fixed day, something that makes Tuesday less empty. Tell someone at home that the quiet days are the heavy ones.[CHIPS]Ideas for weekdays|Is that normal|What helps[/CHIPS]

prompt: my grandmother had alzheimers and i think the missing started long before the funeral
reply: That has a name: anticipatory grief. You mourned the person while she was still here, and then again at the end. It is why the funeral itself may have felt oddly late, or numb. Neither the early grief nor the flat feeling afterwards means you loved her any less.[CHIPS]Is that normal|I feel numb|A memory idea[/CHIPS]

prompt: my best friend from childhood moved away in year six and i still measure friendships against her
reply: Early friendships set a template, and it is a high one; nobody else got those years with you. Measuring is natural, but it can quietly stop new people from getting a fair go. Keep her as a standard for warmth, not as a bar others must clear. And it is not too late to message her.[CHIPS]Should I message her|Making new friends|I miss her[/CHIPS]

prompt: our family dog was fifteen and we knew it was coming, why does knowing not help at all
reply: Because knowing prepares the calendar, not the feeling. You cannot practise an absence; the silence in the house on the first evening is new no matter how long you saw it approaching. Expecting it to hurt less is a very common trap. Fifteen years is a lot of daily life to unlearn.[CHIPS]Is that normal|What helps|I miss him[/CHIPS]

prompt: i keep the last photo of my rabbit as my lock screen and my sister says thats morbid
reply: It is not morbid, it is a photograph of someone you loved. People keep pictures of the dead everywhere: walls, wallets, shrines. Your sister may simply find it hard to see unexpectedly, which is hers to manage, though a quiet word would be kind. Keep it as long as it comforts rather than stings.[CHIPS]Is that normal|What do I say|I miss him[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write something to read at my grandfathers memorial without falling apart
reply:
Write it short and specific: one story, one thing he said, one thank you. Specific is far easier to read aloud than grand.
[STEPS]Pick one true story|Read it aloud three times|Mark a pause before the hardest line|Ask someone to stand beside you[/STEPS]
Crying partway through is completely acceptable, and nobody there will mind.[CHIPS]Help me draft it|What if I cry|Good idea[/CHIPS]

prompt: everything still smells like the hospital and its been weeks since my thatha died
reply: Smell memory is stubborn and it attaches hard to intense days. Some of it is real trace, most of it is your brain replaying. It fades, though not on request. Fresh air, a different soap at home and time all help a little. If the hospital keeps arriving uninvited in your head, tell a parent; that is worth an adult knowing.[CHIPS]Why does that happen|What helps|I miss him[/CHIPS]

prompt: my desk partner changed schools and the seat next to me still feels wrong
reply: Years of small jokes and shared rubbers add up to more than people credit. An empty seat is a daily reminder in a room you cannot leave. Message him, not a big message, just what happened today. And it is worth asking someone new to sit there rather than leaving the gap to speak for itself.[CHIPS]What do I send|Who should I ask|I feel low[/CHIPS]

prompt: i went back to my old neighbourhood and it had carried on completely fine without me
reply: That is a strange, deflating thing to discover, and almost everyone who moves away meets it. Places do not hold a space for us; people do, and they are usually indoors. It does not cancel what happened there. Your version of that neighbourhood still exists, it just lives with you now rather than on the street.[CHIPS]Is that normal|I feel low|A memory idea[/CHIPS]

prompt: my mother gave away my grandmothers plants after she died and i understand why but it still hurts
reply: Both halves of that sentence can be true, and you do not have to pick one. She probably could not face watering them; you wanted something living to keep. Ask whether one is still nearby, because plants get passed to neighbours and relatives and a cutting is often possible. If not, choose one of your own this weekend and grow it in her name.
